What I do: Write the requirements document: purpose, scope, who it is for, what it is NOT for, and 15 competency questions the ontology must be able to answer
Why it comes here: Everything downstream gets checked against these. It is three pages of writing, not code, and it is the highest-value hour available
What exists at the end: requirements.md, and 15 questions that also become my evaluation chapter
Risk if I skip it: I build classes nobody needs and cannot prove the ontology works at the end

What I do: Go through all 42 columns and decide: reuse an existing term or invent one. Check three things that could each save weeks: the CosIng RDF on GitHub, DermO on BioPortal, and Wikidata coverage of my 1,463 brands
Why it comes here: If CosIng already exists as usable RDF, my entire ingredient layer arrives free and cited. Finding that out AFTER building it would be painful
What exists at the end: A 42-row table that goes straight into the thesis, and possibly a free ingredient layer
Which paper told me to do this: LOT and MOMo both put reuse before building; Grau et al. on safe reuse
Risk if I skip it: I reinvent 28,573 ingredient entries that already exist in RDF

What I do: Draw each module as a diagram first, then write the Turtle. core, product, evidence, user, plus the Lebanon file that imports them
Why it comes here: Modules change at completely different speeds. Product data changes weekly, clinical knowledge barely changes. I can hand a dermatologist ONE small file instead of 12,629 rows
What exists at the end: The ontology itself, and the diagrams my thesis chapter needs anyway
Which paper told me to do this: MOMo (Shimizu 2022); Hansanie & Silva did the same and said why
Risk if I skip it: One monolithic file that nobody can review, reuse or update in parts

What I do: Build the long-format helper file (one row per ingredient mention, about 295,991 rows), write the YARRRML mapping, run Morph-KGC, load into GraphDB as named graphs split by source
Why it comes here: This is the step that decides whether this is a METHOD or a script. A mapping file is auditable, citable and rerunnable. Named graphs mean I can reload one source without touching the others
What exists at the end: Roughly 1.8 million triples, and a mapping file for the appendix
Which paper told me to do this: TOXIN used R2RML; Abesova used OntoRefine; Morph-KGC papers
Risk if I skip it: An unauditable script, and no way to trace which source a statement came from

Sprint: 5. Make it think, then check it
What I do: Turn on the defined classes, run HermiT, write the SHACL shapes, run OOPS! and FOOPS!. PREDICT each defined class size first, then compare against what the reasoner actually produces
Why it comes here: Predicting then checking is a real validation step. If SensitiveSafeProduct does not come out near 9,537, my model is wrong and I want to know now
What exists at the end: Evaluation numbers, and the 593 sensitive-marked products containing EU allergens surfacing as a FORMAL inconsistency rather than a note in a README
Which paper told me to do this: Abesova for defined classes; OOPS! and FOOPS! papers; Rahayu on the evaluation gap
Risk if I skip it: I publish an ontology whose defined classes were never checked against reality

What I do: w3id address, WIDOCO documentation, Zenodo DOI. Then answer every one of the 15 competency questions with a SPARQL query and put the query and its result in the thesis
Why it comes here: One of my five criticisms of the existing literature is that almost nothing is published. I cannot make that criticism and then not publish. And the CQ answers ARE the evaluation chapter
What exists at the end: A citable artefact with a DOI, and a complete evaluation chapter
Which paper told me to do this: LOT publication activity; FoodKG and COPPER both publish; Braun 2025 is the template
Risk if I skip it: The thesis ends with a claim instead of an artefact, and the field cannot build on it
